en: Petavatthu,
Mahāvagga 1.
The Story of the Ambasakkara Ghost (Ambasakkara-petavatthu)
There is a city named Vesālī belonging to the Vajjis;
there lived a Licchavi named Ambasakkhara.
Having seen that [being] outside the city,
Seeking the reason for this, he asked him right there:
"He has neither bed nor sitting place;
he has no advancing and no retreating."
He has no enjoyment of food, drink, chewables, or clothing;
he has no female attendants either;
nor does he have any kinsmen, those seen or heard of, or dear friends.
Those who were compassionate toward him in the past do not even get to see him now,
for his self has been purified of that people.
Friends do not remain with one who is untruthful;
friends abandon one they perceive to be deficient.
But seeing his welfare, they surround him.
Many friends have for one who is resolute;
but for one who has fallen low from all his enjoyments—
beaten down and with limbs mangled— it is difficult [to find such].
Like a dewdrop trembling on a blade of grass,
today or tomorrow there will be an obstruction to life.
Such is this state, fallen into the ultimate hardship.
“Terrified by the stake of the *pucimanda* tree, you say:
‘Now, by what reasoning do you speak, O Yakṣa?
Live, sir! Life itself is better.’”
“He was my own kinsman, O King;
I remember him from a former birth.
Upon seeing him, compassion arose within me.”
"May this man of evil character not fall into hell!
Having passed away from here, O Licchavi,
this person shall go to the terrible hell that is filled with sevenfold spikes."
One who performs evil deeds is reborn in a place of great heat, bitter and terrifying;
yet it is many times better [to endure] that than [the consequences of such acts].
This very stake is identical to that hell;
falling into that hell, which is exclusively painful, bitter, terrifying, and absolutely intense.
And having heard these words of mine, he,
overcome by suffering, might give up his life;
therefore, I do not speak in his presence.
“Do not bring about the obstruction of my life.
“This matter of the man is understood;
we wish to ask you about something else as well.”
“If you will not grant us the opportunity, we ask you this; you should not be angry.
“Truly, I gave my promise at that time.”
There is no speaking for one who lacks faith; thinking,
"He will not believe my words against his will," ask me whatever you desire, according to your inclination.
“Whatever I shall see with my eye,
all that I shall fully believe;
even having seen it, I would not fail to believe.”
“Yakkha, you should carry out the act of banishment against me.
“Let this be your word of truth to me:
having heard the Dhamma, may you obtain perfect confidence.”
One who seeks another’s welfare and has no corrupt mind will explain to you every Dhamma— both what you have heard and what you have not heard—
in such a way that they understand it.
“On a horse adorned with trappings,
you approached the presence of one impaled on a stake:
‘This vehicle is wonderful and beautiful to behold;’”
“Whose is this the ripening of that karma?
“In the middle of the city of Vesālī,
on a muddy road, there was a hell.”
With a mind full of faith,
I took a piece of white gośīrṣa sandalwood and placed it in hell;
having set my feet upon this, [I have now attained such a state].
Both we and others have transcended;
this vehicle is wonderful and beautiful to behold—
it is the ripening of that very same karma.
“Your complexion shines forth in all directions,
and your fragrance wafts through all directions;
you have attained the psychic power of a yakkha, O one of great majesty.”
"You are naked; what is the result of this?
"I am free from anger, with a mind always serene, and I approach people with gentle words."
This is the ripening of that very same karma:
my divine complexion shines forth constantly.
And for those established in the Dhamma, there is glory and renown.
Having seen him, I spoke with a clear mind:
"This is the ripening of that very deed;
a divine fragrance wafts from me constantly."
While his companions were bathing at a ford,
he took their clothes on the bank and hid them;
though seeking amusement, his mind was not corrupted.
“Therefore I am naked and my livelihood is difficult.
“They say that such is the ripening of the karma for one who, while playing, commits evil.”
"But for one who performs [an action] without sporting about,
what do they say is the ripening of that karma?
"Those people whose minds are of evil intention..."
Defiled in body and speech,
at the breaking up of the body,
they will undoubtedly go to hell in the life hereafter.
But others, aspiring to a happy destination,
delighting in giving and having integrated their own being,
upon the breakup of the body, in the life hereafter—
“Without doubt they go to a happy destination.
“How may I know for certain this ripening of good and evil?”
"What have I seen that I might believe this?
Or who could make me believe it?
"Having seen and heard it, you shall believe."
This is the ripening of the good and the evil;
if both good and evil were non-existent,
could beings possibly be well-faring or ill-faring?
If mortals here did not perform deeds—
whether good or evil— in the world of men,
there would be no beings who are well-fated or ill-fated.
Low and exalted [beings] exist in the world of humans.
For mortals perform deeds,
both good and evil, in the world of humans.
Therefore, beings in the world of humans— whether well-faring or ill-faring, low or exalted—
are said to be the result of two kinds of kamma.
That which is to be experienced as pleasure and that which is to be experienced as pain—
those deities enjoy them,
while fools, failing to see the duality, are tormented.
There are no deeds performed by oneself;
even after giving, there is none who can assign [the merit]:
clothing, bedding, food, and drink.
“Therefore I am naked and my livelihood is difficult.
“Could there be some means, O Yakkha,
by which you might obtain clothing?”
“Tell me what cause there is;
let us hear the words of a cause that inspires faith.
“There is a monk here named Kappitaka;”
The meditator of virtuous character, the Arahant, is liberated;
with sense faculties guarded and the Pātimokkha restrained,
he has become cooled and attained the supreme vision.
Gentle, generous, well-spoken, and pleasant-faced, of good arrival and easy to converse with,
a field of merit dwelling in a state free from conflict—
He is worthy of offerings from both gods and humans.
He is peaceful, smokeless, free from distress, and desireless;
he is liberated, free from the arrow [of craving], without possessiveness, and without crookedness.
Free from acquisitions, with all conceptual proliferation exhausted, he has attained the threefold knowledge and is radiant.
Though seen, he is not easily known; though heard, he is not easily understood.
They address him as a "Muni";
the yakkhas and bhūtas know him to be free from passion,
one of virtuous nature wandering through the world.
If you, having designated them for me, were to give him one pair or two,
let those be accepted as given to me.
"And see me too, clad in my fine robes.
"In what place does the ascetic dwell?
Having gone there, we shall see him now."
“He who would dispel intoxication, doubt, and perplexity,
as well as the thorns of wrong views—
he is sitting here, Kapinaccana.”
Surrounded by many deities,
he who is truly named speaks a discourse on the Dhamma,
being diligent among his own disciples.
“Thus I shall go now and provide the ascetic with a pair of garments;
let them be accepted by him.”
"And may we see you dressed in armor.
"Do not approach one who has gone forth at an improper time;
O Licchavis, this practice of yours is excellent."
"And having approached at that time,
look right there for him as he sits in seclusion.
Having said "So be it," he went there.
Surrounded by a host of servants,
that Licchavi approached the city and entered his own residence to take up his abode.
Then, at that time, having performed his household duties,
bathed, drunk, and found a moment of leisure,
he carefully selected eight pairs of garments from the basket.
The Licchavi had it dug by a group of slaves.
Having approached that place,
he saw that ascetic of peaceful mind.
Having returned from his alms-round,
cooled and seated at the foot of a tree,
he approached him and spoke to him.
He inquired after his health and well-being:
"In Vesālī, venerable sir,
the Licchavis know me as Ambaṭṭhasakkara."
"These eight beautiful pairs [of garments] are mine;
accept them, Bhante, I give them to you.
It is for this very purpose that I have come here."
“Just as I would be satisfied.
“From afar indeed, recluses and brahmins avoid your dwelling;”
The mats in your dwelling break apart,
and even the outer robes are torn asunder;
then others [are destroyed] by foot-axes.
The ascetics fall headlong;
such harassment as this,
committed by you, the ascetics must endure.
You did not give even a drop of oil from a blade of grass,
nor did you point out the path to the bewildered;
you took for yourself the staff of the blind man.
"Such as you are— miserly and unrestrained—
by what reason, or having seen what,
do you share with us?"
“I confess, venerable sir, what you say:
I harassed both recluses and brahmins;
it was out of a desire for sport, and not with a corrupted mind.”
This too was indeed a misdeed of mine, venerable sir.
Having produced evil through playfulness,
the yakkha experiences suffering, not having completed his enjoyment.
A young man, a sharer in nakedness—
what indeed is more painful than that?
Having seen this, O Bhante, I have attained a sense of spiritual urgency.
Or even for that purpose I give this gift;
please accept, Bhante, these eight pairs of cloths,
so that these offerings may go to the yakkha.
“Truly, giving is praised in many ways;
may there be for you, as you give, the state of imperishability.
I accept from you these eight pairs of garments.”
“May these offerings go to the Yakkha.
Then that Licchavi, having rinsed his mouth,
gave eight pairs of cloths to the Elder.
And they were accepted,
and you saw the yakkha clad in armor;
he saw him smeared with the essence of sandalwood.
Mounted upon a noble steed of magnificent hue,
adorned with ornaments and fine garments,
he was surrounded by yakkhas who had attained great supernatural power.
Thus, seeing that, he was satisfied and uplifted,
with a joyful heart and a beautiful appearance;
and having seen the karma that brings great fruition, he rejoiced.
Having directly perceived it with his own eyes,
he approached him and said,
"I shall give gifts to ascetics and brahmins."
“And there is nothing whatsoever that I would not give you;
you, O Yakkha, have been very helpful to me.
“And you, O Licchavi, are but a small part to me,” [he replied].
"He gave gifts that were not in vain;
I shall now make them fruitful with you as my witness,
O non-human being, together with this human."
“You were my refuge, my kinsman, and my ultimate resort;
you were my friend and my deity.
With palms joined in reverence, I entreat you:”
“I wish, O Yakkha, to see you once again.
“If you should become faithless,
miserly in nature, and possessed of a perverted mind;”
You shall not obtain me for your sight,
and even having seen you, I shall not speak with you; however, if you should be one who respects the Dhamma, [then you may see me].
Delighting in giving, having mastered his own being,
and serving as a wellspring for recluses and brahmins—
in this way you shall obtain a vision of me.
And having seen you, O Venerable One, I shall address you:
"Quickly release me from this stake!
Whatever was the cause for which I acted as a witness..."
I think it was for the sake of one impaled on a stake that we acted as witnesses for one another,
so that this man might be quickly released from the stake.
One who practices the teachings with thorough attention may be released from that hell;
yet there may still be karma to be experienced elsewhere.
Having approached Kappitaka and shared [the food] with him at the proper time,
sit down by his side and ask him yourself with your own mouth.
Thus he will explain this matter to you.
Approach that very bhikkhu and ask him,
seeking knowledge and with a mind free from malice.
"Thus he will explain to you every teaching, both what has been heard and what has not been heard,
according to his understanding. Having conversed there in secret, he—
Having made a superhuman witness,
he departed for the presence of the Licchavis,
and then spoke to the assembled multitude.
“Listen, sirs, to my single word:
I shall choose a boon that will bring me welfare.
This man of cruel deeds has been impaled upon a stake.”
With his staff raised and appearing as one who pursues [his prey],
for this long— namely twenty nights—
he was neither living nor dead because he was obstructed.
“I shall now release him;
let the Saṅgha grant its permission according to its wisdom.
“Release him and others quickly as well.”
"Who can speak to one who acts thus?
Act according to what you understand;
the Saṅgha grants permission according to your own judgment."
So, having approached that place,
he quickly released him from the stake and said to him, "Do not fear, good man."
And he provided for the physicians.
And having approached Kappitaka,
at the proper time, he shared [the food] with him.
The Licchavi, seeking the reason for his condition,
approached him face-to-face and questioned him in that same manner:
"A man of cruel deeds has been impaled on a stake."
With his rod laid aside and his nature free from malice—
for this duration of twenty nights,
being thus restrained, he neither lives nor dies.
"Having been thus released by me and now gone,
O Bhante, because of this yakkha's words,
could there perhaps be some underlying reason?"
Tell us, venerable sir, if there is a cause by which he would not go to that hell;
we wish to hear words concerning the cause that may inspire confidence.
“There is no destruction of those kamma-actions;
there is no reaching their end here without experiencing them.
“If one were to practice those things...”
If one is heedful and reverent day and night,
one may be released from that hell,
though there may still be karma to be experienced elsewhere.
“This purpose of the man has been understood;
now, O Bhante, have compassion for me as well.
Instruct me, advise me, O one of vast wisdom.”
“May I not fall into hell.
“This very day, with a mind full of confidence, go for refuge to the Buddha, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha.”
In the same way, undertake the five steps of training,
unbroken and flawless.
Quickly refrain from taking life.
In this world, avoid taking what is not given;
do not drink intoxicants, nor speak falsehoods,
and be content with your own wife.
And undertake this noble, excellent eightfold path,
which is wholesome and brings about happiness:
[the practice of] robes and almsfood, and...
Requisites such as bedding and seats;
food, drink, hard foods,
and likewise clothing and dwellings.
Give with a mind full of serene confidence to those who have become upright,
and also to the bhikkhus who are perfected in virtue.
To one who is free from passion and learned,
satisfy them with food and drink;
thus merit always increases.
And practicing these qualities in this way,
being diligent and attentive day and night,
you shall be released from that hell.
“Kamma might be experienced elsewhere.
“This very day, with a mind full of confidence, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.”
In the same way, I undertake the five steps of training, unbroken and flawless.
I shall quickly abstain from the taking of life.
In this world, I avoid taking what is not given;
I do not drink intoxicants, nor do I speak falsehoods,
and I am content with my own wife.
And this noble eightfold path, endowed with excellence,
which is wholesome and results in happiness, I undertake:
robes and almsfood, and...
Requisites such as bedding and seats;
food, drink, hard foods,
and likewise clothing and dwellings.
To monks endowed with virtue,
free from passion, and learned,
I give; I do not waver.
“Delighting in the teaching of the Buddhas.
Such was the Licchavi Ambasakkhara,
a certain lay follower in Vesālī.
The bhikkhu, faithful, gentle, and diligent in his duties,
then served the Saṅgha with great care.
And he who had been impaled on a stake became free from disease.
Serī, seeking happiness, went forth into homelessness;
and by relying on the monk Kappita, the supreme one,
they both attained the fruits of recluseship.
Such is the service of true persons for the wise who understand it: it yields great fruit.
Even one pierced by a stake attained the highest fruit.
But the youngest son honored Ambasakkara.
This is the first story of the ghost Ambasakkara.
